title: Application of unsupervised machine learning to identify and characterise hydroxychloroquine misinformation on Twitter
screen_reason: Published in the Lancet Digital Health 'Comment' section, but it is not commentary: it reports an original empirical analysis of 2,771,730 tweets collected from the Twitter streaming API on 'hydroxychloroquine'/'chloroquine' keywords, 21-30 July 2020, and gives the share of the reviewed tweets identified as containing misinformation topics with an explicit numerator and denominator (1,044,794 of 1,237,999; 84.4%). A share of items in a sample classified as misinformation = CONTENT. Kept despite the journal's section label; see the judgement notes for the two things that qualify it (a machine-selected denominator and a very loose numerator definition).

estimates.country: Not stated (global public Twitter stream; the episode analysed is US-centred - a retweet by then-President Trump)
estimates.date: 21-30 July 2020 (pre-period 21-26 July, post-period after Trump's 27 July retweet)
estimates.measure_type: % of reviewed hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine tweets and retweets identified as including hydroxychloroquine misinformation topics
estimates.denominator: 1,237,999 tweets and retweets reviewed (174,600 pre-period + 1,063,399 post-period), which is 44.7% of the 2,771,730 tweets collected on the keywords 'hydroxychloroquine' and 'chloroquine' from the public Twitter streaming API, 21-30 July 2020; the reviewed set is those tweets correlated to biterm-topic-model clusters plus the top 100 retweeted tweets of each period
estimates.definition: Tweet text assigned to one of four thematic misinformation categories - rumours (treatment); prevention and treatment (clinical treatment, folk medicine); authority action and policy (general, media management, medical measures); conspiracy - with categories adapted from previous COVID-19 misinformation studies and applied by manual annotation of tweets correlated to the BTM clusters
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper works from the WHO infodemic definition - "an overabundance of information, including deliberate attempts to disseminate wrong information to undermine public health response" - and states in its disclosure that "The classification of posts as 'misinformation' tweets is a matter of independent assessment and opinion, rather than fact, informed by other peer-reviewed articles that similarly classified misinformation COVID-19 topics."
estimates.page_loc: p. e74, concluding paragraph ("Most (84·4%) of the 1 237 999 tweets reviewed contained misinformation"); first stated in the Results, p. e73 ("After analysing the content, 1 044 794 (84·4%) of the 1 237 999 reviewed tweets were identified as including hydroxychloroquine misinformation topics."); category breakdown in Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Unsupervised biterm topic model (BTM) clustered tweet text; the authors then reviewed the thematic groups for relevance to misinformation topics and manually annotated tweets correlated to those clusters against categories adapted from prior COVID-19 misinformation studies; embedded links were checked against the assigned theme. 'Authors coded posts independently and achieved high intercoder reliability (kappa = 0.92) and met and conferred on correct classification for discrepancies by reconsulting misinformation categories.' The category assignment for the full 1.04 million tweets is necessarily propagated from cluster membership, not annotated tweet by tweet.
estimates.moderator_quote: we first collected Twitter posts from the public streaming Twitter application programming interface from July 21–30, 2020, using "hydroxychloroquine" and "chloroquine" as keyword filters. ... After using the BTM and extracting the top 100 retweeted tweets we were able to review 174 600 tweets and retweets from the pre-period and 1 063 399 tweets and retweets from the post-period, constituting 44·7% (n=1 237 999) of the entire dataset.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR - three things drive this number upward and should be visible wherever it is used. (1) DENOMINATOR IS MACHINE-SELECTED: the 84.4% is a share of the 44.7% of the corpus that BTM clustering surfaced plus the top-100 retweeted tweets, NOT of the 2,771,730 tweets collected. Over the whole collected corpus the implied share would be at most 1,044,794/2,771,730 = 37.7%, but that is a complement-style computation I did not keep as a row (R8). Coded denom_selection=curated for this reason. (2) NUMERATOR IS VERY LOOSE: the four categories include 'authority action and policy related to media management' (19.1% of the coded dataset) and 'authority action and policy related to medical measures' (13.5%), which capture tweets ABOUT censorship and policy rather than tweets asserting a false claim; the authors themselves disclose that the misinformation classification is 'a matter of independent assessment and opinion, rather than fact'. Hence breadth=misleading rather than false. (3) GROUND TRUTH IS A HYBRID: coded researcher_coding because the misinformation judgement and the kappa = 0.92 are human, but the label reaches 1.04 million tweets through unsupervised BTM cluster membership - an extractor who codes this 'classifier' would not be unreasonable, and the ground_truth_detail carries the full mechanism. Also note the paper is a 'Comment', a section label, not a commentary genre. QUOTE NOTE: the Lancet two-column layout interleaves the columns in the extracted text, so neither full sentence survives as a contiguous span; the source_quote is the longest contiguous fragment that carries both the value and the denominator, and the full sentences are reproduced in page_loc.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) PRE/POST SPLIT NOT GIVEN ITS OWN ROWS - collapsed to the single representative point (the overall 84.4%) per the instruction to collapse time series. The verbatim components, should an adjudicator want them: 'Overall, there was a lower proportion of misinformation tweets observed in the pre-period (136 963 [78·4%] of 174 600 tweets) versus the post-period (907 831 [85·4%] of 1 063 339 tweets).' Note the post-period denominator is printed as 1,063,339 here but as 1,063,399 two paragraphs earlier - a 60-tweet typo in the paper; 907,831/1,063,339 = 85.38%, so the smaller figure is the one the percentage was computed on. (2) TABLE 1 CATEGORY SHARES not extracted as rows: rumour (treatment) 400,486 (32.4%), prevention and treatment - clinical treatment 16,365 (1.3%), folk medicine 12 (<0.1%), authority action and policy general 97,995 (7.9%), related to media management 236,491 (19.1%), related to medical measures 167,616 (13.5%), conspiracy 125,830 (10.2%). These are mutually exclusive sub-types of the headline number (they sum to exactly 84.4% of 1,237,999) - i.e. sub-rows of a pooled figure, excluded per the unit-of-analysis rule. DATA-QUALITY FLAG: within Table 1 the 'percentage of coded dataset' column is computed on 1,237,999 (400,486/1,237,999 = 32.4%) while the pre- and post-period columns are computed on the misinformation counts of each period (109,012/136,963 = 79.6%; 291,474/907,831 = 32.1%), so the three columns of the same table do not share a denominator. 'Crisis situation updates' and 'Stigma' rows are empty. (3) '56 879 (5·4%; from 49 082 unique users) of 1 044 794 tweets that were identified as including misinformation-related topics expressed concern about hydroxychloroquine misinformation or introduced information about the potential risks' - the denominator is the misinformation-only set but the NUMERATOR is corrective counter-speech, not misinformation, so it is not a falsity share and R3/within_misinfo_content does not apply; no row. (4) '2 523 766 tweets (91·1% of the entire dataset) collected in the post-period' is a volume split, not a misinformation share. (5) 'these misinformation tweets and retweets were liked ... 2 193 021 times by 283 055 unique Twitter users' - bare counts with no denominator of users or of likes, so no REACH or SHARING row is possible (a REACH row would need the share of users reached). (6) Poster metadata (average 2,294 followers, following 1,644, account age 5.5 years) is descriptive, not a share. (7) No concentration statistic is reported: the paper never states a top-X% of users or sources accounting for a Y% share, so R1 cannot be met.

rob.design: Infoveillance study of the public Twitter streaming API, keyword filters 'hydroxychloroquine' and 'chloroquine', 21-30 July 2020, bracketing Trump's 27 July retweet of the Breitbart/America's Frontline Doctors video; 2,771,730 tweets collected. Unsupervised biterm topic modelling (k chosen by coherence score) grouped tweet texts; thematic clusters were reviewed for relevance to misinformation, tweets correlated to those clusters were retrieved and manually annotated against categories adapted from two previous COVID-19 misinformation studies, and the top 100 retweeted tweets of each period were added; embedded links were checked against the assigned theme. 1,237,999 tweets (44.7% of the corpus) were reviewed. Reliability as reported: authors coded independently, kappa = 0.92, discrepancies resolved by conferring. Stated limitations: single platform, and no assessment of whether accounts were bots or commercial. Author-declared conflict: three authors are employees of S-3 Research, an NIH/NIDA-funded startup. Raw data cannot be shared under Twitter terms; tweet IDs are public on GitHub. Principal risks for this review: the analysed denominator is a machine-selected 44.7% subset of the corpus, the misinformation categories include policy/media-management topics rather than only false claims, and the authors state the classification is assessment and opinion rather than fact.
rob.item6_quote: Manual annotation was done to identify thematic misinformation topics on the basis of the unit of analysis, which was the text of each tweet reviewed, with categories adapted from previous studies on COVID-19 misinformation (appendix pp 8–10).
rob.item10_quote: After analysing the content, 1 044 794 (84·4%) of the 1 237 999 reviewed tweets were identified as including hydroxychloroquine misinformation topics.
